Stated Claim / Post Context:
Nashville grocery tax cut: How much you can save starting this weekend

The effective local rate on food drops to 2.25% saving the average family an estimated $72 a year.

Actual Article Body:
What This Story Is About

Why It Matters

What Happens Next

Catch Up

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - The average Nashville family will save an estimated $72 a year when Davidson County’s effective local grocery tax rate drops to 2.25% on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Metro is cutting its share of the grocery tax by half a percent under a new state law that allows cities to lower their tax rates on certain categories. The cut equals a nickel on every $10 spent at the grocery store.

The local grocery sales tax will fall from 2.25% to 1.75% to cancel out the additional 0.5% people pay on every purchase for the Choose How You Move transit initiative.

“We’re giving you this investment back in one of those areas that we know every family has those basic household costs,” Mayor Freddie O’Connell said.

The reduction applies to food and food ingredients. It does not apply to alcoholic beverages, tobacco, candy, dietary supplements or prepared food.

O’Connell included the tax cut as a proposal in this year’s budget. Metro Council approved the plan in July to eliminate around $9 million in spending to cover the change.

City and state leaders have been working since then to enact the lower tax rate just on groceries, allowing the change to take effect on Sunday.

“Every family in Nashville will notice when they look at their receipt after buying groceries,” O’Connell said. “This is millions of dollars in tax breaks to Davidson County residents.”

O’Connell said the savings may be small at first, but are designed to compound over time.

“In week one, it might only be a few bucks. But over the course of the year, it might really add up to an entire trip of groceries,” O’Connell said. “You are spending that money on the things that you need rather than on just taxing a basic necessity.”

Shemaiah Lee, a single mom, said she wonders at the Kroger checkout whether she has enough food stamps to cover the bill. Lee said grocery prices have continued to climb along with things like rent and gas.

“That sounds like that would be really helpful for me,” Lee said of the change. “Things are priced really high recently, and it’s been hard for me to afford things even with food stamps.”

John Hinger said the price of groceries is going up, and his only way to stay within his means was cutting down on what he buys.

“It’s a baby step in the right direction,” Hinger said. “Right now, I got to lose weight. Eating less will save me money. It’s a win-win proposition for me.”

Jeff Castleberry said he welcomes a reduction in taxes but wants to make sure other taxes do not go up to cover the cut.

“It’s nice to know that the city once in a while engages in reducing a tax as opposed to the other direction they usually take in raising them. I’m sure quite a few people will be happy to hear that,” Castleberry said.

Castleberry said the amount saved from a half-percent cut is small but still “appreciated very much.”

O’Connell said he is looking at lowering Metro’s grocery tax rate again next year if the budget allows. He wants the state to also help by looking at the 4% tax it charges on groceries.

“We would love to work with the state of Tennessee to offer more of this at no cost to Tennesseans. That is what we are pushing for next,” O’Connell said.

O’Connell said he’s hoping to one day eliminate the grocery tax but a lot of that will depend on rising costs the city is paying, like employee healthcare coverage.
